books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

primary_sources: 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 23; Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.9

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 23, and Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.9: In the summer of 1932 thousands of unemployed World War I veterans marched on Washington to demand early payment of bonuses legally due them in 1945. After clashes with police left two veterans dead, President Hoover ordered federal troops to clear the veterans from downtown Washington. General Douglas MacArthur went further than his orders, storming the veterans’ camp on the Anacostia River with fixed bayonets and tear gas. The shelters were burned and dozens were injured.

stem: The Bonus Army episode most damaged Hoover's standing because it

options.text: proved the veterans had been paid in full
options.misconception: The veterans had not been paid. Their bonuses were due in 1945, and Hoover and Congress rejected early payment.

options.text: showed federal troops used against unemployed veterans
forced Congress to pass the New Deal
options.misconception: The New Deal came under Roosevelt in 1933. Congress passed no New Deal because of the Bonus Army.

options.text: ended the Great Depression within weeks
options.misconception: The Depression continued for years after the summer of 1932. The episode changed no economics.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Hoover and Congress rejected the veterans' demand, so the bonuses stayed unpaid until 1945.
rationales.B: Background from the books: MacArthur stormed the veterans' camp with fixed bayonets and tear gas, and the image of soldiers attacking former soldiers angered Americans.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the New Deal was Roosevelt's program, beginning with the Hundred Days of 1933, not a result of the Bonus Army.
rationales.D: Background from the books: unemployment peaked in 1933, the year after the march, so the Depression was far from over.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what Americans saw: federal troops driving out unemployed veterans.
2. Ask how that looked: soldiers attacking the men who had served in the last war.
3. Ask what it cost Hoover: trust, since he already seemed out of touch.
4. The episode damaged him because it showed troops used against veterans.
Remember: a picture can cost a president more than a policy, so ask what the public saw.
